Title: IRS official who refused to testify facing more scrutiny over scandal, past
Summary:
Lois Lerner has become a lightning rod in the scandal over the Internal Revenue Service targeting tea party and other conservative groups. In 2012, Lerner was given the job of heading up the Exempt Organizations unit in the IRS's tax exempt division. Lerner is an experienced IRS attorney with experience handling cases involving politically active groups. On May 10, 2013, the New York Times reported that conservative nonprofit groups were being held back by the IRS while it sorted through their applications. Lerner responded to questions about the matter during a meeting of the American Bar Association Tax Section Conference in Washington on May 10, stating “There’s absolutely no targeting.”
Background: When IRS Director Steven Miller appeared before members of Congress on May 22 to discuss the improper targeting of conservative groups, he blamed the actions of lower level employees in Cincinnati. That explanation fell short of satisfying many. At least part of the reason for that might be found in the fact that some of the officials responsible for reviewing applications from conservative groups were given the job after being placed in charge by career civil servants. That includes Lois Grossman Lerner – who was named head of the IRS Exempt Organization Unit last year. The Exempt Organization Unit reviews applications from groups applying for exemption from federal income taxes. According to reports in the Wall Street Journal, the unit started rejecting or delaying applications from conservative groups in 2010. According to the newspaper, the unit began singling out applicants whose applications included terms such as “Tea Party” or “Patriot,” and demanded detailed information about donors.
Legal experts say that Lerner, who has worked for the IRS for 20 years, may qualify for constitutional protection from self-incrimination. She could still be subpoenaed to appear and give testimony, however, which could result in criminal contempt charges and fines if she refuses to cooperate.

NYC mayor backs gay marriage referendum vote in Maine
By KATHLEEN RONAYNE 9 hours ago
PORTLAND, Maine (AP) -- New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg has become the latest high-profile official to endorse a same-sex marriage ballot measure in Maine that could give momentum to a national drive to put the question before voters.
Bloomberg announced Wednesday he had donated $100,000 to the campaign to keep the measure off the ballot and ensure its passage should it make it there. The measure would allow same-sex couples to marry in the Pine Tree State and it's up for a vote at the November election.
"It's very important to me," Bloomberg told reporters at a news conference in Portland. "I think it's really the right thing to do. ... It's just the fair thing to do."
Maine will join five other states where voters will decide whether they want to authorize same-sex marriages, including California, which already passed such a proposal last month. Minnesota and Washington state will also consider the issue. In Oregon, residents rejected a constitutional ban in November.
Several Republican candidates for president have expressed misgivings with the measure. Rick Santorum, a former Pennsylvania senator, has vowed to overturn same-sex marriage laws nationwide if elected. Mitt Romney, the former Massachusetts governor, supports the Maine initiative.
Gov. John Baldacci, a Democrat, said he was disappointed in Bloomberg's decision because the campaign is "about democracy, not one person's private political preferences."
Opponents say the measure could lead to polygamy and that children raised in same-sex households suffer more health problems. Supporters argue it would help homosexual couples get equal treatment.
"We've been treated terribly for so many years," said Jesse Connors, a spokesman for Yes on 1. "We haven't been given the opportunity for full participation in our society, and we deserve that opportunity."

Between 2011 and 2014, researchers examined a nationally representative group of 1,615 sixth-, eighth-, 10th- and 12th-graders. As many as one in five kids reported having tried an e-cigarette. That's compared with just 1 percent reporting cigarette use during the same period.

In this case, you are comparing the candidate’s annual tax rates over several years. To do so accurately, you must compare apples to apples. If one candidate’s returns show annualized net capital gains rates (that is, if the taxes they paid on capital gains are lower than the standard tax rate) then your comparison should be against what that candidate would have been paying in taxes had they not received those capital gains.
When writing about tax returns, reporters often cite figures such as “their average effective tax rate” or “their marginal tax rate.” Those are useful figures only for explaining how much income someone’s taxes consume compared to everyone else, but they aren’t the correct numbers to report when you need to compare candidates.
To compare two candidates’ tax returns, simply compare the bottom lines on each candidate’s Form 1040 (page 1). That will tell you exactly how much money they paid in taxes. If a candidate’s net taxes were significantly different than another candidate’s, ask why.
Taxes can have many effects on the candidate beyond just how much they pay in taxes. For instance, taxes affect the value of the stock options a candidate may receive. Tax rates also affect how much capital a candidate must invest before they qualify for tax credits (income below a certain threshold is tax free under current law), and it might even affect where a candidate chooses to live (some states offer significant tax breaks for moving there, like Texas does).

Employees are often given the ability to choose their hours and/or their work locations. Increasingly, corporations have discovered that remote workers can be very productive while saving money on overhead costs such as office space, utilities and commuter fees. Telecommuting has been around for years and is no longer a radical concept; in fact, most large companies now offer telecommuting options to employees. Workers can choose when they want to work, where they want to work and how they want to work. Companies can save upwards of $20 billion annually just through reductions in lost workdays due to illness. Employees may find that they can achieve better results during lesser peak traffic times rather than trying to navigate the crowds every day.
While there are certainly many challenges involved with implementing telework arrangements, the benefits typically outweigh the drawbacks and may actually be cheaper in the long term.
To ensure success, both parties will need to share responsibilities regarding technology tools and information security. It’s important to keep in mind that telework doesn’t always mean working alone. The USCCB has taken a stand on several issues, including health care reform, financial regulation and immigration policy. On almost every issue (except foreign policy), the bishops have followed the lead of Catholics in Alliance for the Common Good, whose goal is to make American society more just, peaceful and humane. Although many in the media and elsewhere may have forgotten it, the USCCB is essentially an alliance between progressives and social justice advocates, including both religious and secular organizations. This alliance has created the impression that the bishops, especially in matters involving economics or poverty, are on one side of the political divide. That view, while understandable, is incorrect, and the bishops are now moving to counter that perception.
In short, the USCCB has long opposed policies that harm the most vulnerable citizens, whether through racism, sexism or classism. In the past few weeks, the bishops have explicitly stated their opposition to any budget cuts targeting programs for the poor. As I wrote yesterday, they will take the same position during the debate over raising the debt ceiling. They oppose any budget measures that endanger the environment or threaten peace. Their position on health care reform is simply that the current bill does not go far enough in helping Americans, while their position on immigration reform is based on the belief that immigrants should be welcomed and that undocumented workers should be protected from deportation. This is the position of Catholics in Alliance; it is not surprising, therefore, that it represents the official position of the bishops.
To clarify how these statements can fit together, one must understand that the bishops are an umbrella organization. Some of its members are liberal while others are conservative, just like other groups in the coalition. Because they recognize that no matter how different their views on, say, abortion might be, they still share common goals, principles and interests. Those commonalities have caused some conservative bishops to criticize the bishops for taking positions on certain issues that are contrary to their own personal stances. To the detriment of everyone involved, however, those voices will always remain outside the room where the actual bishops meet—the conference. The conference is much more than the sum of its parts. It is something greater—a coalition working together toward a better society.

The U.S. Supreme Court will decide whether to hear arguments in two lawsuits aimed at undoing the Affordable Care Act, or Obamacare, after the justices ruled Monday that they would take no further action on the cases.
After meeting behind closed doors for three hours, the nine justices voted unanimously Monday not to intervene in two separate federal appeals court cases involving the health care reform law. Both cases were brought by the state attorney generals, with Texas leading the charge against the law.
The court will now allow the appeals courts to continue to resolve the issues presented by the lower-court rulings striking down key parts of the law, including its individual mandate provision requiring most Americans to carry health insurance.
In both cases, the appeals courts upheld a district judge’s decision declaring key provisions of the law unconstitutional under the Commerce Clause. However, the Fourth Circuit Court upheld the law based on the Constitution’s Tax Clause, giving it authority to issue a tax penalty for failing to obtain health coverage. The D.C. Circuit upheld the law only as applied to the individual mandate and struck down the entire law if the mandate was removed.
In the Supreme Court’s order issued late Monday, the justices agreed to stay an injunction issued by the D.C. Circuit Court against the Health and Human Services Department until it rules on whether to grant expedited review. The four liberal justices dissented, arguing that the stay should not be granted. They noted that the D.C. Circuit Court had already stayed its own injunction pending appeal.
The health care law continues to face legal challenges even as it starts being implemented next year. A decision by the Supreme Court could come this summer.

Title: Obama Boehner Fiscal Cliff Meeting: Grasping For Last-Minute Solution
Summary:
In what may be the most significant budget showdown of the year, Republicans and Democrats began formal negotiations Thursday over how to avert the so-called fiscal cliff. President Barack Obama sent his team of negotiators - Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner and his senior adviser on economic issues Gene Sperling - to meet with House Speaker John Boehner's team early in the morning. Both sides said they hoped to reach an agreement by Dec. 21, when Congress recesses for the holiday season. But Republicans want more concessions before they will even begin negotiations. House Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy, R-Calif., said that if Democrats agree to extend the Bush-era tax cuts on all income levels through next year instead of only the middle class, they would be willing to start talks. Without any compromise from Democrats, Boehner said he would continue to seek input from members of the GOP conference over the weekend as to whether he should keep pushing for an agreement or let the higher tax rates expire for all Americans. On Wednesday, House Republicans voted down a bill that included lower income tax rates and the extension of other tax provisions such as the Research & Development Tax Credit.
Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., also suggested Republicans won't start talks until they get a promise from Democrats that they won't raise tax rates on those making less than $400,000 per year. If they do agree to extend current rates on everyone except high-income earners, negotiations could begin quickly as both parties look to try to work something out before the holiday break. But any effort to get an agreement before Congress goes on break could be difficult because Republicans would like more time to finish legislation to repeal what they call Obamacare and Democrats have not indicated that they would agree to a deal that includes that provision.
The day's developments marked the beginning of a delicate give-and-take between the White House and Congress as they scramble to strike a deficit reduction deal, which will determine the fate of the nation's economy, tax code and health care system.

Title: Sparks fly as Biden, Ryan face off in feisty vice presidential debate
Summary:
In a head-to-head battle of proxies, Vice President Joe Biden spent most of the evening Thursday fighting fire with fire in a scrap with Rep. Paul Ryan that often resembled the sparring that took place between President Barack Obama and GOP vice presidential nominee Rep. Paul Ryan a week earlier. But on the crucial questions on Medicare and Social Security reform, Biden came up short.
Both candidates offered some new lines. Biden repeated a line he used during Monday's debate (and one he may use again in the future), asking Ryan whether he wants to "go back to the philosophy we had when Ronald Reagan was president, where we looked out for Wall Street before Main Street?"
And after Ryan tried to paint himself as a frugal government employee, Biden reminded him of his own career at the Heritage Foundation, saying "you guys wanted to privatize Social Security. You didn't want any responsibility at all for it."
Ryan was much more focused than Obama, hitting Biden directly instead of simply criticizing his boss. This approach resulted in a bit more tension and the occasional smile breaking out, as the two men frequently traded jabs.
Biden was aggressive, even though he was the older man who has been in Washington longer. He sought to turn every question into an attack on Ryan's record. And he wasn't shy about reminding viewers that he is the person standing in Obama's stead; he kept saying, "I'm the guy sitting right here..."
It was a good strategy, but as several pundits noted, Biden was left looking small when he got too personal -- like when he tried to mock Ryan's claim to have never taken a congressional earmark, pointing out he was in Congress for 10 years and never asked for anything. When Ryan pointed out Biden never asked for money for a hospital in Scranton either, Biden appeared a bit rattled.
In terms of substance, Ryan was able to get away from the word "government" and explain the differences between his plans and the president's. Even Biden's point about Ryan's lack of experience wasn't effective, given that Biden was making the same charge against Obama.

Title: Donald Trump Is Sworn In as President, Capping His Swift Ascent
Summary:
As Mr. Trump stood on the inaugural platform and prepared to take the oath, the scene below him offered a striking contrast between the incoming president’s appeal and the Obama presidency, which was leaving office amid widespread unhappiness.
On the Mall were scattered protesters, a few holding placards denouncing Mr. Trump and his views. A larger number of demonstrators massed in downtown streets, dwarfing the sparse crowd for Mr. Trump’s swearing in.
At the same time, a much larger crowd than gathered in 2009 to see Mr. Obama take the oath flocked to downtown streets. Hundreds of demonstrators carrying signs that read “No! Not My President!” clashed with thousands of people dressed in the black T-shirts and red baseball caps bearing Mr. Trump’s name.
Protesters had hoped to gather inside the grounds of the Capitol, but the architectural review commission rejected their request because they wanted to install 200 “jail cells,” a wooden structure meant to resemble a prison with a chain-link fence around it.
Members of Congress appeared on the steps of the Capitol after listening to the invocation by Rabbi Marvin Hier of the Simon Wiesenthal Center, who asked for divine assistance as the nation faces threats from abroad and a leadership void at home.
Singer James Taylor performed “America the Beautiful,” and cellist Yo-Yo Ma played “Simple Gifts.” Then came Carole King singing “You’ve Got a Friend,” as videos showed images of Mr. Trump throughout his life.
Finally, Chief Justice Roberts administered the oath using a 1797 edition of the Constitution that once belonged to Alexander Hamilton. Mr. Trump kept his hand over his heart during the ceremony until he finished reciting the oath, then he put his hands together and bowed his head to listen to a minister offer a prayer.
He delivered his speech standing before a platform covered with white roses, beside a large American flag draped down the entire length of the Capitol, with others lined up on the floor behind him.
Mr. Trump promised that “from this moment on, it is going to be America First,” referring to the isolationist movement that opposed entering World War II. His message was aimed at those who voted for him.

Analysis: The federal government operates on a 12-month budget cycle. Every fall, the president must submit a proposed budget for the next fiscal year (October 1 through September 30). However, the government continues its routine activities, without interruption, during this period. Instead of cutting the checks for the coming year immediately after the president's budget submission, lawmakers wait until the new fiscal year begins. They then pass legislation authorizing additional expenditures for the coming fiscal year. These bills typically contain some language delaying their effective date, so that there will still be time remaining in the old fiscal year when they take effect. That way, spending for both the current and upcoming fiscal years can occur within the same calendar year. Thus, when the president signs such a bill into law, he actually signs two separate pieces of legislation. The first provides authorization for the current fiscal year, while the second provides actual appropriations for the coming fiscal year. In essence, the first bill authorizes what is called "continuing resolution" authority, while the second provides for the appropriated funds themselves.

After several years of debate among policymakers and researchers over whether social media companies should be regulated under Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act (CDA), they will soon find out. On January 30th, Attorney General William P. Barr sent a letter to several large tech companies informing them that their Section 230 protections would no longer be automatically granted. Instead, these companies now have 30 days to submit evidence of why they deserve these protections. In the letter, Barr notes that “Section 230 immunities are proper and appropriate when applied to good actors doing a good job, but improper and inappropriate if given to bad actors who knowingly facilitate criminal activity.”
Background: The Communications Decency Act (CDA) was part of the Telecommunications Act of 1996. Among many things, the CDA established that Internet platforms would not be treated as publishers or speakers of information users posted online. As a result, they would not be liable for defamation claims arising from third party speech on their platforms. It did so by giving Internet companies broad immunity from civil liability on their platforms for material posted by third parties unless the company was aware of the specific offensive post. If so, then the company must take steps to prevent further publication of the objectionable content. However, due to this immunity provision, courts were hesitant to hold companies accountable for defamatory posts.
In April 2018, Congress amended Section 230(c)(1) of the CDA. Under Section 230(f)(5)(B), courts are directed to assess “whether the activity allegedly constituting a violation occurs on or off platform, and whether the company is directly profiting from its operation.” This amendment allowed for greater scrutiny of how companies handle user speech. Specifically, it allows courts to determine whether a company’s business model relies on the facilitation of offensive third-party content.

Title: House approves sweeping Dem election reform bill, amid First Amendment concerns
Summary:
In 2005, Senators John McCain (R-Ariz.) and Russ Feingold (D-Wis.) introduced legislation to amend the U.S. Constitution and create new limitations on the nation’s elected officials. Proponents claimed that the proposed constitutional amendment would limit lobbying and eliminate corruption through restrictions on how members of Congress could accept gifts and fundraising contributions. However, analysts found that, despite its name, the proposed legislation did little to protect the nation’s democracy from corrupt activities. Instead, they said the proposal gave the impression that corruption was already limited when, in reality, many types of corruption were still legal. Analysts noted that the proposal came at a time when Congress had recently enacted several laws that addressed lobbying practices, including the Honest Leadership and Open Government Act of 2007. Moreover, a number of other bills designed to address corruption at the state and federal levels were being considered. Proponents argued that their proposal offered protection against corruption that existing laws lacked, but analysts concluded that the proposal would have added another layer of bureaucracy to the nation’s anti-corruption laws without changing much about what was already prohibited under current laws.
Issue: Corruption has a long history in the United States, though the federal government does not publish statistics on corruption cases that occur at the state level. President Abraham Lincoln, who suspended habeas corpus during the Civil War, was accused of authorizing illegal wiretapping and warrantless searches. The New York Times reported in 2005 that the number of corruption convictions declined between 1986 and 2004, while the number of convictions on financial crimes increased during that same period. However, there is no comprehensive source of data on corruption convictions, especially those related to ethics violations.
Legislative Context: The McCain-Feingold Lobbyist Ethics Bill was part of a series of major campaign finance reforms proposed or enacted since 2002. WASHINGTON (AP) _ An unemployment rate of just under 5 percent is close to what most economists consider full employment. So why can't there be enough workers to fill all the job openings?
The unemployment rate fell to 4.9% in January from 4.8% in December, the Labor Department reported Feb. 2. About 6.1 million jobs were available then _ 230,000 more than in November, which had been the lowest total since April 2000.
Yet the number of unemployed people actually rose _ from 6.6 million in December to 6.9 million in January. That means the unemployment rate fell even though the number of unemployed increased.
That's because the ranks of employed people swelled to 155.2 million, the most since the end of World War II, while the work force shrank to 155 million _ also the most since the 1940s. The civilian labor force, which excludes children, students and retirees, fell by more than half a million people in January.
Why? Because millions of Americans are giving up looking for work or settling for less than full-time schedules _ either out of choice or necessity, said Heidi Shierholz, an economist at the Economic Policy Institute, a liberal think tank.
For example, a surge in low-wage jobs has made people reluctant to quit higher-paying positions, and the increase in part-time employment could reflect a preference for flexibility or the need to support families on only one income, she said. Another factor: Workers sometimes stay away when governments shut down some services.
"It doesn't mean that workers aren't willing and able to work," Ms. Shierholtz said. "They don't want to accept the wages and working conditions that go along with those jobs."
If the ranks of the unemployed keep rising, economists worry about the weakening economy because consumer spending accounts for more than two-thirds of U.S. economic output. Many forecasters predict a mild recession later this year as the global economy slows.

Summary:
When Trump says ‘much’ or ‘a lot,’ he means ‘a little.’ Or, probably, he doesn’t know and just makes it up.
Nearly all of Trump’s statements today were misleading, false or both. He used the words much (4), lots (6) and very often (2). As usual, they weren’t true.
Of course, in some cases, Trump didn’t even pretend to be telling the truth. The president has long claimed to be an expert on the U.S.-Mexico border, even though he lacks anything approaching a rudimentary understanding of the issue. And yet in public appearances, he constantly blunders when questioned by reporters about such details as how long the border is or where he thinks the best place to put the wall is.
Trump’s claim this week that the border wall is almost finished comes as no surprise. The president is incapable of admitting failure, which explains why he continues to push for something that most Americans believe is unnecessary ― and perhaps, given the lack of evidence for its effectiveness, counterproductive ― even though he’s been unable to make progress.
What’s really remarkable, however, is that Trump and his supporters can actually believe that the wall is nearly done ― despite the fact that it hasn’t been started.
There’s also the issue that Trump’s assertion is contradicted by his own Department of Homeland Security. The department’s most recent status report, issued earlier this month, listed only 22 miles of new wall construction completed. A December report found the same thing.

This article reports the results of a study comparing the effects of school start times on student achievement, attendance rates, and safety and health indicators.
The researchers looked at all 4,992 public high schools and 3,333 middle schools in the United States. They found that later start times were associated with higher test scores, better attendance rates, and lower rates of students getting hurt, being bullied or having suicidal thoughts.
The findings show that delaying school start times can significantly improve educational outcomes.
Studies have shown that teenagers’ sleep schedules tend to fall behind as they grow older. Many teenagers get less sleep than recommended each night. Even though teenagers need plenty of sleep during regular school hours and extracurricular activities, most schools have traditional early start times—usually around 7:30 AM or earlier.
This study compared average test scores at schools that started school at different times. Specifically, the authors found that the average SAT score at schools starting at 8:30 AM was 14 points higher than at schools beginning classes earlier.
Similarly, the study found that the average ACT composite score was 4 points higher at schools starting after 8 AM versus those that began before 8 AM.
The authors also found that attendance rates tended to be slightly higher at schools starting at 8 AM or later. However, there wasn’t a clear trend showing whether late start times resulted in better academic performance overall.
Late starts did lead to slightly worse classroom behavior and teacher ratings of engagement and participation. However, these differences may not be significant enough to change how educators teach students.
Overall, the authors concluded that later start times led to higher academic achievement and decreased risky behaviors among adolescents.
In addition to benefiting teens directly by reducing morning grogginess and boosting energy levels throughout the day, later start times may help prevent car accidents involving tired drivers. According to CDC data reported by USA Today in September 2018, teen fatalities from motor vehicle crashes dropped by nearly 40 percent when states moved high schools back an hour or more during the past decade.

Full Article: Motherhood Isn't Holding Women Back in the Workplace After All (Mindy Levy, Time)
Research has shown that once a woman has a child she may receive less pay, fewer opportunities for advancement and less job security. This study suggests that the negative effects do not begin until a woman is actually expecting her first child.
Due to changing family structures, more young women are working while raising children and many couples share responsibility for child care. However, women who do not bear children still shoulder the majority of domestic labor, such as shopping and cleaning. For many, having children may simply be viewed as additional domestic burden rather than something that will increase demands on professional life.
In this study researchers found that only women without young children were significantly less likely to remain employed after having a baby. In fact, women with very young children were almost twice as likely to stay in the labor market as those with older children. These findings underscore the importance of policies that offer greater flexibility for both men and women, especially fathers, to take time off to spend time with children. Policies that allow both parents to take advantage of work/family programs also show promise for making work arrangements more flexible and equitable.
The research was published in the February issue of Social Science Research.

Title: Obama: ‘In God We Trust' Vote Not Creating Jobs

A number of countries use In God We Trust on their currency. Its origin is disputed, but several theories exist.
Why the phrase was selected is unknown.
Some credit former Treasury Secretary Daniel Raymond, whose first name is sometimes misspelled as Dennis. Others credit Raymond Timoshenko, the Russian-born director of the Mint. Still others credit the sculptor of the Lincoln Memorial, Felix de Weldon. One thing most agree upon is that Raymond had a hand in selecting the phrase.
Another theory points to George Washington as the inspiration for the phrase; it may have come from his Farewell Address of 1796. Washington wrote, “Of all the dispositions and habits which lead to political prosperity, Religion and morality are indispensable supports.” Some believe Washington’s use of the word “morality” means that America should be governed by religious principles.
The phrase appeared in two different versions before it was chosen by the Commission of Fine Arts in 1908. Both versions were submitted by Raymond, who reportedly changed the words slightly.

Summary:
In an effort to curb government spending, Congress is considering a range of options including changing Social Security benefits. The White House and leading Democrats oppose such plans, while Republicans insist it’s their only alternative if they want to bring down the federal deficit.
Background: Since 1935, Social Security has provided benefits to retired people and those disabled from work. It takes money from current workers’ salaries to provide money for the elderly through monthly checks or, for some, through monthly benefits paid directly to health care providers. Over the years, Congress has allowed those retiring at younger ages than originally intended to qualify for retirement benefits. In addition, there are those who receive a disability benefit because they can no longer perform certain tasks. Overall, more than one-third of the U.S. population is eligible to receive a monthly check.
Who it affects: About 56 million Americans are eligible to receive Social Security benefits; they are also likely to collect Medicare coverage, the entitlement program available to everyone over age 65. Seniors are a large and vocal voting block and politicians try to avoid angering them. But if the program falls into financial crisis—as it may well by 2035, when the trust fund is expected to run dry—retired people might see their benefits reduced or eliminated altogether.
What to watch: If Republicans win control of either chamber of Congress after November elections, they could seek substantial reductions in Social Security and Medicare benefits. If they don’t control either house, they might seek to eliminate the payroll tax for upper earners.

Summary:
Donald Trump is threatening to throw away his power as a kingmaker within the Republican Party unless the party nominates someone who can win over independents and Democrats. He also says there should be a third-party candidate in the general election.
Donald Trump says he has no intention of leaving the field empty for the general election against President Barack Obama, asserting Wednesday that a strong third-party candidate should emerge from the crowded Republican primary campaign.
Trump’s comments came a day after he announced that he would end his months-long role as “kingmaker” in the 2012 presidential race by stepping aside from hosting a November Republican debate at the Reagan library outside Los Angeles.
Without Trump’s participation, there were concerns that the debate would lack star power among the most prominent contenders in the Republican field. But Trump said Wednesday that without any other candidates agreeing to join him, there would have been no point holding such a debate, which was already scheduled well into October. Instead, he plans to announce his own choice for the top nominee next week.
He did not say whether he would be endorsing one of the candidates or whether he thought one of them could win enough support from independent voters and Democrats to capture the White House. A Trump endorsement could significantly boost a candidate’s fundraising and national profile.
“I think you’ll find it interesting when I pick somebody,” Trump said during an appearance on CNN’s “The Situation Room With Wolf Blitzer.” He added later, “I think it’s going to be good news, because I don’t want it to look like I’m backing somebody because I’d rather see a little bit of competition, OK?”
When asked about whether there could be room for two candidates from the same party in the fall election, Trump responded, “We need somebody that people respect, and that they want to vote for, so I guess we’re going to have to wait and see what happens.”

Title: Vicente Fox, Ex-President of Mexico, Scoffs at Donald Trump’s Visit
Summary:
Donald Trump’s trip to Mexico will make headlines, but what really matters about the trip may be what comes out of it—if anything at all. Here’s why it might go wrong.
Donald Trump is heading to Mexico on Wednesday to meet with President Enrique Peña Nieto, but one of the Mexican leader’s predecessors had a different message for the Republican presidential nominee: You are not welcome here.
The trip itself is significant for several reasons. The Republican frontrunner is going to the land where so many illegal immigrants have gone before him, and he says he wants to help Mexico solve its problems. What could possibly go wrong?
There are already plenty of things to worry about. If Mr. Trump were to offer any kind of apology, even if it wasn’t sincere, then that would likely be enough to spark a reaction from the left wing of the Democratic Party.
But while there is no shortage of other concerns—like whether Mr. Trump is serious or not, or if he will continue to make statements that antagonize certain groups, such as Muslims and African-Americans, and whether he actually believes the claims he makes about immigration—there is nothing more threatening than an unprepared candidate stumbling into a foreign country where he thinks he knows everything and saying, essentially, “Hey guys, I’m your best friend.” That happens when someone does not do their homework, or does not listen to their advisers, or both.
Of course, Mr. Trump might get lucky. He could come up with the perfect statement, a message that resonates, appeals to voters of all stripes, and is remembered long after it is forgotten by the news media.
Or maybe he won’t say much at all, preferring instead to focus on the handshake he exchanged with the Mexican president last summer when they were together in Cuba for Mr. Obama’s summit with the leaders of the region. (That was awkward.)
It’s possible that the first day of his trip will go smoothly. But if things take a turn for the worse, Mr. Trump could end up looking foolish—and potentially cost himself a shot at the White House.

What does it mean when someone asks you if your name is on something? It means they are saying they own it or they authorized something. It doesn’t mean they’re bragging about what they have. That would be boastful.
To be clear, you didn’t sign anything saying your name is on anything, did you?
No, of course not! You were simply asked if your name appears anywhere on anything. If it is, then tell him that it is, but only where you’ve consented to having it appear. Tell him exactly where it is and why you agreed to let it be there.
Then tell them about the time you had dinner with them, and they took off their shoes while in your house. Ask yourself how often do you take off your shoes while in other people’s houses? Now ask them if they’ve taken off their shoes while visiting others, and if so, who are those others. See if they remember.
If they say yes, ask them what makes them think that anyone else would want to invite them back into the house after seeing them barefoot. They should be ashamed of themselves, because no one is proud of being embarrassed.
Now, imagine what you would tell them if they weren’t your friend anymore. Would you be talking about taking care of your childhood friends or getting rid of your ex-boyfriend?
You see, we can’t always get along with everyone. So don’t try to force a friendship unless you know it will last forever. There are many reasons you might need to separate from someone you thought was your best friend.
For instance, if you’ve ever been betrayed by someone you loved, you might feel that they aren’t trustworthy any longer. Or maybe your family member did something bad or wrong with you. Maybe you got robbed or cheated on by a former partner or coworker.
Whatever the reason may be, never fear, it isn’t the end of the world. Keep working hard at fixing things between you and your ex. Remember that some relationships don’t work out because they just weren’t meant to be together in the first place. Some people are better apart than together. But most of all, never give up hope! Love conquers all!
